meaning: One adjusts something, the other takes it on.

items.meaning: To change something so it fits a new situation.
To take something on and start using it.

difference: You adopt a thing as it is; you adapt it to make it fit.

examples.sentence: We adopted Go and adapted our tooling around it.
The template needs adapting for each region.

remember: 'Adoption' is the noun for take-up; 'adaptation' is the noun for change. Both appear constantly in product writing.

meaning: One is entry, the other is too much.

items.meaning: The right or ability to enter or use something.
An amount beyond what is needed or allowed.

difference: Access lets you in; excess is a surplus.

examples.sentence: Only two people have production access.
Anything in excess of the quota is charged separately.

remember: 'In excess of' is a formal way of saying 'more than'.

meaning: One evaluates, the other informs.

items.meaning: To assess the value or quality of something.
To inform someone of something.

difference: You appraise a thing; you apprise a person.

examples.sentence: Please apprise the team of the change.
The surveyor appraised the property at half a million.

remember: 'Appraisal' is the common noun — a performance appraisal evaluates, it doesn't inform.

meaning: Three similar words for blocking, detecting, and criticising.

items.meaning: To remove content considered unacceptable.
A device that detects a physical change.
Formal, official criticism.

difference: A censor blocks, a sensor detects, and censure condemns.

examples.sentence: The logs are censored to remove personal data.
The temperature sensor reports every ten seconds.
The committee issued a formal censure.

remember: 'Censure' is criticism, not removal. Being censured and being censored are very different outcomes.

meaning: Three homophones for quoting, place, and vision.

items.meaning: To quote a source as evidence.
A location — physical or on the web.
The ability to see, or something seen.

difference: You cite a source, visit a site, and lose your sight.

examples.sentence: The report cites three independent studies.
The site went down at two in the morning.
The end is finally in sight.

remember: 'On-site' means at the physical location. 'Cite' appears mostly in academic and legal writing.

meaning: One is about a climax, the other about climate.

items.meaning: Relating to the most intense or decisive moment.
Relating to weather and climate.

difference: Climactic is drama; climatic is weather.

examples.sentence: The climactic scene lasts eight minutes.
Climatic conditions delayed construction.

remember: The extra 'c' in climactic comes from 'climax'.

meaning: One works together, the other confirms.

items.meaning: To work jointly with others.
To confirm a claim with independent evidence.

difference: Collaborating produces work; corroborating confirms a claim.

examples.sentence: The two teams collaborated on the design.
We need a second source to corroborate this.

remember: Corroboration must be independent. Two people repeating the same source corroborate nothing.

meaning: One shows contempt, the other deserves it.

items.meaning: Showing scorn towards someone or something.
Deserving to be scorned.

difference: The contemptuous person looks down; the contemptible thing is looked down on.

examples.sentence: He gave a contemptuous shrug.
Blaming a junior for it was contemptible.

remember: The '-ible' ending means 'able to be', which is why contemptible is the one that receives the scorn.

meaning: One is believable, the other believes too easily.

items.meaning: Believable; worth taking seriously.
Too willing to believe things without evidence.

difference: A credible claim deserves belief; a credulous person gives it too readily.

examples.sentence: It's a credible threat and we should act on it.
The scam targets credulous first-time investors.

remember: 'Credibility' is what you build; being credulous is a weakness. Same root, opposite value.

meaning: One removes danger, the other spreads out.

items.meaning: To make a dangerous or tense situation calmer.
To spread out over a wide area; or, as an adjective, unfocused.

difference: Defuse removes the fuse; diffuse spreads.

examples.sentence: She defused the tension with one question.
Responsibility is too diffuse — nobody owns it.

remember: 'Defuse the situation' is the common phrase, and 'diffuse the situation' is the common error.

meaning: One marks something obsolete, the other loses value.

items.meaning: To mark as outdated and discourage use — technical.
To fall in value over time — financial.

difference: Software is deprecated; assets depreciate.

examples.sentence: That endpoint is deprecated and will be removed in v3.
The hardware depreciates over four years.

remember: Deprecated code still works — it's discouraged, not removed. That's the whole point of the warning period.

meaning: The same move, seen from each country.

items.meaning: To leave your country to live elsewhere.
To come into a country to live there.

difference: You emigrate FROM a country and immigrate TO one.

examples.sentence: She emigrated from Ireland and immigrated to Canada.
Thousands emigrated in the 1950s.

remember: E for Exit, I for In. The prefixes carry the direction.

meaning: One is stated, the other is understood.

items.meaning: Stated directly and clearly.
Understood without being stated.

difference: Explicit is said; implicit is implied.

examples.sentence: Let's be explicit about who owns this.
There's an implicit assumption that traffic stays flat.

remember: Implicit assumptions cause most planning failures — making them explicit is the whole value of a design review.

meaning: One means officially, the other means previously.

items.meaning: In an official or proper manner.
In the past; previously.

difference: Formally is how; formerly is when.

examples.sentence: The change was formally approved on Tuesday.
The service was formerly known as Atlas.

remember: 'Formerly known as' is the standard phrase for a renamed product or company.

meaning: One is a stockpile, the other is a crowd.

items.meaning: A hidden store of things — or to accumulate them.
A large, often unruly crowd.

difference: A hoard is things; a horde is people.

examples.sentence: He hoards old hardware in the server room.
A horde of support tickets arrived after the outage.

remember: Panic buying causes hoarding, not hording — a common headline error.

meaning: One is unbelievable, the other is disbelieving.

items.meaning: So remarkable it's hard to believe.
Unwilling or unable to believe something.

difference: The thing is incredible; the person is incredulous.

examples.sentence: The turnaround was incredible.
She was incredulous when she saw the invoice.

remember: Same pattern as credible/credulous — the '-ulous' form always describes the person's state of mind.

meaning: One means reluctant, the other means hate.

items.meaning: Reluctant; unwilling. An adjective.
To hate intensely. A verb.

difference: Loath is mild reluctance; loathe is strong hatred.

examples.sentence: I'm loath to refactor this close to release.
I loathe meetings without an agenda.

remember: The silent e makes it a verb — the same pattern as breath/breathe.

meaning: One is about ethics, the other about mood.

items.meaning: Relating to right and wrong; also the lesson of a story.
The confidence and spirit of a group.

difference: Moral is about ethics; morale is about how a team feels.

examples.sentence: Team morale is low after the reorganisation.
There's a moral argument as well as a legal one.

remember: The stress differs: MOR-al but mor-ALE. That difference is what the extra e signals.

meaning: One is a viewpoint, the other means potential.

items.meaning: A point of view or way of seeing something.
Expected or potential in the future.

difference: Perspective is how you see; prospective is what might come.

examples.sentence: Three prospective clients are in the pipeline.
From a support perspective, this is a big change.

remember: 'Put it in perspective' means judge its real importance compared with other things.

meaning: One oppresses, the other takes to court.

items.meaning: To treat someone cruelly over a long period, often for their identity.
To bring legal proceedings against someone.

difference: Persecution is oppression; prosecution is a legal process.

examples.sentence: The company was prosecuted for the data breach.
The group was persecuted for decades.

remember: Getting these wrong in any legal or HR context is a serious error — they make very different accusations.

meaning: One means study closely, the other means to tip liquid.

items.meaning: To examine something closely — always 'pore over'.
To make liquid flow out of a container.

difference: You pore over documents; you pour a drink.

examples.sentence: We pored over the logs for three hours.
Pour the sample into the second container.

remember: 'Pouring over the logs' is the common error — and an odd image.

meaning: One is quiet, the other is unwilling.

items.meaning: Not willing to talk or reveal much.
Unwilling to do something.

difference: Reticent is about speaking; reluctant is about acting.

examples.sentence: He was reticent about why he left.
The client was reluctant to sign without a discount.

remember: 'Reticent to do something' is widespread but strictly wrong — reticence is about silence, so use 'reluctant'.

meaning: One is a compliment, the other is not.

items.meaning: Not complicated — usually positive in design and writing.
Oversimplified, ignoring important complexity.

difference: Simple is praise; simplistic is criticism.

examples.sentence: It's a simple solution and it works.
That's a simplistic view of why customers leave.

remember: Calling someone's design 'simplistic' when you meant 'simple' turns a compliment into an insult.

meaning: One means in words, the other means spoken.

items.meaning: Expressed in words — which can be spoken or written.
Spoken aloud, not written.

difference: Verbal covers all words; oral covers only speech.

examples.sentence: We had an oral agreement, nothing in writing.
Verbal reasoning is part of the assessment.

remember: 'A verbal agreement' is used everywhere to mean an unwritten one, though strictly 'oral agreement' is the precise term.
